title.narrative: Peace Direct, Unga fred och säkerhet, 2019-2022
Peace Direct, Youth, Peace and Security, 2019-2022

description.narrative: Peace Direct aims to build upon the agency, capacity and effectiveness of young people and communities most affected by conflict and working to build peace. Identified organisations that share the same values and approaches with Peace Direct are given opportunities to design their own initiatives that are contextually appropriate and locally owned. This way Peace Direct avoids being prescriptive on what work youth-led organisations should be doing, allowing them instead to take the lead to develop their own strategies and ideas to tackle the root causes of violence. The aim of the intervention is to strengthen the peacebuilding roles played by young women and men and support them to reduce violence in their communities. Through an initial mapping and feasibility study of five geographical areas where Peace Direct already is active, namely DRC, Mali, CAR, Nigeria and Pakistan, three to four projects will be initiated that will strengthen the role of young peacebuilders in their communities based on their different identified needs and priorities. Support will vary from strengthening the organisations’ capacities to providing targeted small grants to peacebuilding initiatives and supporting in-country convenings of local organisations to exchange on relevant topics that aim to build peace locally.

Peace Direct arbetar med lokala grupper av människor för att förhindra våld och bygga hållbar fred baserat på en uppfattning om att lokala problem kräver lokala lösningar och lokalt ägande. Det Sida finansierade projektet Youth Action for Peace ger Peace Direct en möjlighet att arbeta med unga fredsbyggare i konfliktdrabbade områden genom att stödja lokalt identifierade och kontextuellt anpassade aktiviteter som gynnar fred och fredsbyggande eller genom att stärka ungdomsledda gruppers interna styrning utifrån deras egna behov. Genom finansiella bidrag har de unga fredsbyggarna möjlighet att utföra sina egna innovativa, kontextspecifika aktiviteter, utan påverkan från givare eller internationella organisationer. Projektet inspireras av Säkerhetsrådsresolution 2250 om unga, fred och säkerhet och den studie som gjordes, ”The Missing Peace”, som bland annat lyfter vikten av att skapa möjligheter för unga människor att forma sin egen agenda för deltagande i ämnen som berör även dem.

Peace Direct works with local people to stop violence and build sustainable peace based on the belief that local issues require local solutions and ownership. The approach builds upon strengths and successes to deliver more impact for conflict affected communities through the power of local action. The Sida-funded project Youth Action for Peace will allow Peace Direct to work closely with young peacebuilders in conflict affected areas either by supporting locally identified and contextually suitable activities that favor peace and peacebuilding or by strengthening the organizational capacity of youth-led groups based on their targeted needs. Along with a small grants programme, the young peacebuilders are able to implement their own activities, without being directed by donor or INGO preferences, and address conflict issues in innovative, context-specific ways. The project is inspired by Security Council Resolution 2250 on youth, peace, and security and its progress study “The Missing Peace”, that among other things highlights the importance of creating space for and allowing young people to shape their own agenda for participation in the politics which affect them.

sector.narrative: Civilian peace-building, conflict prevention and resolution

description.narrative:
Based on Peace Directs experience from working with local peacebuilding, with the belief that local challenges require local solutions and ownership, and their interest in advancing the Youth, Peace and Security agenda, Sida decided to support the Youth Actions for Peace project (YAPP) that focused on:
- Improving social cohesion
- Addressing local conflict drivers
- Promoting the role of youth in PB and local decision-making
Peace Direct believes that those who are directly impacted by conflict are best placed to seek out and implement solutions, if only they are afforded the resources, decision-making power, and space to do so. YAPPs flexible funding model enabled 218 emerging young peace actors whether individuals, informal groups, or registered organisations to design and manage innovative peace projects in the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Mali and Pakistan. These projects were grounded in young grantees own lived experience of conflict, embedded in their communities, and adapted to rapidly changing and nuanced local conflict dynamics.
Initial phase
Based on their prior work with locally led peacebuilding organizations, five geographical areas were selected during an initial nine-month phase consisting of contextual analysis and mapping of potential organisations that would be able to take on the role of Hubs for the youth-led peacebuilding initiatives. The analysis showed that youth in the selected areas raised social and political conflicts, gender-based violence, land disputes and lack of employment as common challenges facing youth. Also common for all areas was the perception of exclusion of young women and men from decision-making processes.
Out of the initial mapping exercise, five organisations were selected in CAR, DRC, Mali and Pakistan who already were established civil society organisations. Peace Direct (PD) assessed the organisations internal management and control prior to signing contracts and held initial meetings and training sessions on the Participatory Action Learning Mobilisation (PALM) methodology to be applied with the aim to increase locally led initiatives, ownership and social accountability.
The Hub organisations kept local communities informed about the initiative, managed applications for small grants and closely accompanied grant recipients by providing them with training on project management and mentoring, helping them formally register their organisations and set up bank accounts where necessary, and assisting them to receive further funding from donors.
In total, 218 initiatives were implemented with 948,687 USD, reaching 305,293 people directly and 950,375 indirectly. While the aim of the small and micro grants was catalytic, set up to jumpstart change and be a spark that the youth and community groups could grow from and build on, PD noted many positive outcomes in terms of long-term effects related to community ownership, continuity, unexpected collaborations, increased capacity of both hub and local grant recipients, and strengthened social cohesion and trust between youth and decision-makers in the communities.
By allowing young women and men design their own projects, programming addressed the intersection of several conflict drivers through for instance income generation, intercommunity dialogue and social cohesion. Examples of initiatives are listed below:
Improving social cohesion
CAR: Peace awareness campaigns to promote peace and social cohesion between Christians and Muslims which resulted in Muslim community coming back as traders to central market.
DRC: Pig breeding that brought together Hutu, Tutsi and Nande youth to work alongside each other, addressing both lack of development/food insecurity and inter-ethnic tensions. This further resulted in beekeeping and a community mill to grind pig feed, run by ex-combatants.
Mali: Repair of dyke addressing irrigation and flooding of rice fields as well as integrating conflict management and community building between groups that had been in conflict; addressing literacy of women and girls by installing solar lights, which encouraged local entrepreneur to support by donating additional lights.
Pakistan: Girl-led action to provide solar panels for girls schools, which in turn led to parents, teachers, school management and community to continue to invest in maintenance and operation.
Addressing local conflict drivers through community peacebuilding mechanisms
CAR: Peace concerts through African Music School, using music to raise awareness of the peace agreement and to promote social cohesion. Inspired by the positive response, more parents enrolled their children as it unites people from different backgrounds and develops talents of young people that in turn inspires their peers.
DRC: Peace Huts to manage differences between Hutu and Nande groups; peace clubs created by 50 youth leaders; youth-led early-warning mechanism set up through WhatsApp; Peace Oath signed by students to counter violent demonstrations traditionally taking place at university campuses; inter-institutional committee set up to manage disputes; and radio plays addressing conflict drivers.
Mali: Anti-trafficking training for local chiefs; inter-caste dialogue on slavery shifting perceptions and acknowledgment of universal human rights, among others leading to conservative leaders renaiming neighbourhood that had been called slave quarter; training of journalists on managing fake news and investigating conflict between farmers and cattle breeders.
Pakistan: Youth peace centre for inter-ethnic youth, particularly girls; animated videos and social media campaign to create platform for inclusivity of marginalised youth and raise awareness on impact of discrimination, and television film and radio campaigns to promote peaceful coexistence; Art to express minority Hazara experiences. The initiative received national attention and artist is now seen as icon and role model in her community; Peace Library for school and out-of-school children on co-existence, and storytelling and publication of childrens storybook to promote gender equity; creative arts project with Afghan refugees and host communities to counter extremist values; Speak Karachi bringing university and madrassa religious seminar students together for healthy debates on topics such as discrimination towards minorities and human rights violations against transgender people. The inititative built bridges across differences through creating a youth network of 25 ambassadors from ten institutions. USAID followed up with two rounds of support (50 000 USD) to replicate the project at a bigger scale.
Promoting the role of youth in peacebuilding and local decision-making
CAR: Increasing connections and communication between youth peacebuilders and leaders through 2022 Central African Republic Youth Agenda; radio and TV messages on peacebuilding activities by young women and men.
DRC: local committee composed of local youth council and local chiefs set up to analyse ongoing conflict and engender commitment to peace; partnership with Youth Parliament and elections of 32 local youth councils; organisation of a Peace Exchange that led to Provincial Government and Mayor of Bukavu making public commitments to support the advancement and sustainability of youth-led peace initiatives.
Mali: broadcast of videos to promote youth in peacebuilding; Youth Exchange and Youth Advocacy workshop with former Youth Minister and 300 participants discussing community security and intercommunity dialogue; social integration of IDPs, particularly women, into community. Local authorities now turn to the youth organisation for continued work with the IDPs.
Pakistan: Two female participants of Speak Karachi were selected to work with Parliamentarians on the CVE bill and the Chairman of CDAs Board of Directors was appointed to serve as one of 33 members of National Youth Council; inclusive space (Aman Chaupal) for community gatherings created since mosques had replaced these traditional spaces, thus excluding other religions and minority groups. Local landowner donated piece of land and community influencers provided in-kind support for the construction. Youth were commended for being at the forefront of honouring a past tradition. This was also the first time women were included in community discussions. Proposal put forward to District council to replicate the initiative in 235 union councils; Peace Exchange Youth Resolve for Democracy and Peace brought together youth with Minister of Human Rights and Minority Affairs, senators and national and provincial assemblies.
International advocacy
In addition, Peace Direct also worked on international advocacy by meeting with policymakers in the US and the UN to address barriers against youth inclusion, by encouraging decision-makers to provide youth with necessary resources to lead initiatives for positive change through more inclusive and flexible funding models. This resulted in policy recommendations for Youth Policies, international webinars and publication of reports, among others in partnership with the UN Secretary General Envoy on Youth.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
